```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE)
library(here)
library(tidyverse)
library(knitr)
library(kableExtra)
here::i_am("README.qmd")

# kableExtra styling and the vector figures are LaTeX-only; the GitHub README build
# takes plain pipe tables and the PNG copies.
latex_out <- knitr::is_latex_output()

out <- function(f) read_csv(here("maintained", "output", f), show_col_types = FALSE)
# value_paper holds the string the article prints, thousands separators and all, so it
# is read as text rather than re-guessed into a double that would print 225.000.
gt <- read_csv(here("ground_truth", "kirkland_coppock_2018_ground_truth.csv"),
               col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character(), .default = col_guess()))
published_claims <- read_csv(here("ground_truth", "published_claims.csv"),
                             col_types = cols(value_paper = col_character(),
                                              .default = col_guess()))
manifest <- read_csv(here("original_manifest.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)

chi <- out("text_observational_chisq.csv")
adv <- out("text_observational_experience_advantage.csv")
dataset <- out("text_observational_dataset_description.csv")
corr <- out("text_mturk_yougov_correlation.csv")
pearson_archive <- corr$correlation[corr$method == "pearson" &
                                      corr$specification == "archive (YouGov unweighted)"]
pearson_weighted <- corr$correlation[corr$method == "pearson" &
                                       corr$specification == "YouGov weighted"]

n_extracted <- nrow(published_claims)
n_claims <- nrow(gt)
n_verifiable <- sum(!is.na(gt$match_rewrite))
n_match <- sum(gt$match_rewrite == 1, na.rm = TRUE)
n_miss <- sum(gt$match_rewrite == 0, na.rm = TRUE)
n_paper_internal <- sum(gt$defect_locus == "paper_internal", na.rm = TRUE)
n_archive_locus <- sum(gt$defect_locus == "archive", na.rm = TRUE)
n_descriptive <- sum(gt$table_figure == "Descriptive")
n_descriptive_hold <- sum(gt$table_figure == "Descriptive" & gt$match_rewrite == 1,
                          na.rm = TRUE)
n_descriptive_fail <- sum(gt$table_figure == "Descriptive" & gt$match_rewrite == 0,
                          na.rm = TRUE)
n_no_threshold <- sum(gt$table_figure == "Descriptive" & is.na(gt$match_rewrite) &
                        is.na(gt$defect_locus))
n_a1_absent <- sum(str_starts(gt$claim_id, "table_a1_") & is.na(gt$match_rewrite))
n_paper_internal_descriptive <- sum(gt$defect_locus == "paper_internal" &
                                      gt$table_figure == "Descriptive", na.rm = TRUE)

# The errata spine, written by errata.qmd. Every count of the corrections below reads it,
# so the README and the note cannot come to disagree about how many there are.
spine <- read_csv(here("errata_entries.csv"), show_col_types = FALSE)
n_errata <- nrow(spine)
n_errata_descriptive <- sum(spine$class == "definition")
n_errata_numeric <- n_errata - n_errata_descriptive

# The figure estimates the errata note quotes, read here from the same output files rather
# than typed, so the account of the note below cannot go stale either.
pol_np <- out("figure_3_mturk_main_candidate_pref.csv") |>
  filter(panel == "Nonpartisan", coef_group == "Pol. Experience", !is.na(estimate))
mturk_rep_asian <- out("figure_5_mturk_het_fx_candidate_pref.csv") |>
  filter(panel == "Nonpartisan", coef_group == "Race", party == "Republicans",
         label == "Asian")
competence_diff <- out("figure_7_mturk_het_fx_competence.csv") |>
  filter(panel == "Difference", coef_group == "Pol. Experience", !is.na(estimate)) |>
  mutate(clears_zero = conf.low > 0 | conf.high < 0)
n_per_party <- sum(competence_diff$party == "Democrats")
n_clears_dem <- sum(competence_diff$clears_zero[competence_diff$party == "Democrats"])
n_clears_rep <- sum(competence_diff$clears_zero[competence_diff$party == "Republicans"])

# The prose below spells small counts out.
spelled <- function(n) {
  words <- c("one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight", "nine", "ten")
  if_else(n >= 1 & n <= 10, words[n], as.character(n))
}

fig_img <- function(stem) {
  here("maintained", "output",
       paste0(stem, if (latex_out) ".pdf" else ".png"))
}
```

*Drafted by Claude Opus 5 under the supervision of Alex Coppock.*

This repository holds the actively maintained replication code for Kirkland and Coppock (2018), together with the reproducibility report that documents what the original archive did and did not do. It is part of a program applying the maintenance proposal in Peer, Orr and Coppock (2021, *PS: Political Science & Politics*, doi [10.1017/S1049096521000366](https://doi.org/10.1017/S1049096521000366)) to a set of published archives.

| | |
|---|---|
| Article | [10.1007/s11109-017-9414-8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11109-017-9414-8) |
| Replication archive | [10.7910/DVN/WSUHI3](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/WSUHI3) |
| Pre-analysis plans | none |

**The data are not redistributed here.** The deposit lives at Harvard Dataverse and that is the only copy this repository points at. `download_original.R` fetches it and verifies every file; `original_manifest.csv` records the Dataverse file identifiers, the UNF of each ingested data file, and two checksums per file: the MD5 of the bytes Dataverse serves, which is what this code was written against, and the MD5 Dataverse publishes. Here the two agree for all `r nrow(manifest)` files. They do not always, so the script verifies against the served bytes and reports any disagreement. Either way the exact bytes are pinned in version control even though the bytes themselves are not.

**`recovered/` is different and is committed.** The observational analysis behind Table 1 depends on a data file and a script that the deposit does not contain, though its own README lists both. The authors supplied them, and since they exist nowhere else this repository carries them.

**Repository layout.** `maintained/` is the maintained rewrite: one script per published table or figure, writing to `output/`, which is committed so a reader can compare a fresh run against it without downloading anything. `ground_truth/` ties every published number to the code that produces it, starting from `published_claims.csv`, an extraction of every numeric token in the article and the online appendix. `maintained/in_text_claims.R` prints each of those numbers beside the sentence that states it. `original/` is created by the download script and is deliberately absent from the repository. `errata.qmd` renders `kirkland_coppock_2018_errata.pdf`, a short note listing the article's misstated numbers, and writes `errata_entries.csv`, the one place each correction is written down, which this report counts from rather than keeping its own tally. This README is the reproducibility report, also available as a PDF in `report/`.

**License.** CC0 1.0 Universal, matching the terms of the deposit this repository maintains, so nothing in the chain is more restrictive than the archive itself. See `LICENSE`.

**To reproduce.** Clone or download the repository, open `kirkland_coppock_2018.Rproj`, and run:

``` r
source("run_all.R")
```

That fetches the deposited archive from Dataverse, verifies its `r nrow(manifest)` checksums, produces every published table and figure into `maintained/output/`, rebuilds the ground truth table from those outputs, prints every published number beside the sentence that states it, and verifies the deposit again. It takes about a minute. Individual scripts can be run on their own in any order; only `ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R` and `maintained/in_text_claims.R` depend on the others having run first.

Required packages: tidyverse, estimatr, knitr, kableExtra, here. Paths resolve through `here`, so nothing depends on the working directory and the scripts work equally well under `Rscript` outside RStudio. A successful run overwrites `maintained/output/`, which is committed: **`git diff` on that folder is the reproduction check**, and the CSV and PNG output should come back byte-identical. The eleven PDF figures always show as changed, because a PDF records the time it was written; compare their PNG twins instead.

## Paper Overview

**Citation**: Kirkland, P. A. and Coppock, A. (2018). Candidate choice without party labels: New insights from conjoint survey experiments. *Political Behavior*, 40(3), 571--591.

**Research question**: When a ballot carries no party label, what do voters use instead? The paper argues that without the partisan shortcut voters fall back on other indicators of fitness for office, political experience above all.

**Design**: Three pieces of evidence. An observational record of `r format(dataset$n_elections, big.mark = ",")` US mayoral elections held between `r dataset$year_first` and `r dataset$year_last` across `r dataset$n_municipalities` municipalities, comparing the political experience of winners under partisan and nonpartisan ballots. Then two conjoint survey experiments running the same design on different samples: an MTurk convenience sample (N = 1,204) and a nationally representative YouGov sample (N = 1,200). Each subject judged five successive elections between two candidates whose race, gender, age, career experience, political experience and, in half the elections, party were fully randomized. Outcomes are candidate choice and a 0 to 100 competence rating. Estimation is OLS with standard errors clustered by respondent, and effects are compared across election types by interacting every attribute with an indicator for the nonpartisan ballot.

**Main finding**: Political experience carries substantially more weight when the party label is withheld. In the MTurk sample the political experience coefficients are about 10 percentage points larger in nonpartisan than in partisan elections, and the same interaction appears in the YouGov sample. The competence ratings move the same way, which is the paper's evidence for the mechanism it proposes. The two samples' estimates correlate at `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_archive)`.

---

## Summary

Two questions, answered before the detail.

### Does the deposited archive run?

Not as deposited, and the reasons are all about files rather than about code.

**The YouGov data cannot be loaded under the name the scripts use.** The deposit contains `yougov_replication.xlsx`. It is not a spreadsheet: it is an RData binary carrying the wrong extension, uploaded that way and served that way ever since. Both scripts that need it call `load("yougov_replication.rdata")`, so `yougov_replication.R` and `compare_samples_replication.R` fail on their first data line. Renaming the file, or loading it under its real name, fixes both, and the extension is the whole of the problem: the bytes are a valid RData file and `load()` reads them without complaint.

**Three of the twelve files the archive's README promises were never deposited.** The README lists `observational_mayors_replication.rdata`, `observational_replication.R` and `observational_codebook.txt`, along with CSV copies of all three data files. The Dataverse record has ten files and none of those six are among them. Table 1 and the paragraph of observational results that follows it therefore cannot be reproduced from the deposit at all. The authors supplied the missing data and script separately; they are in `recovered/` and the rewrite reads Table 1 from there.

**Every data path in the archive is mis-cased.** The scripts call `load("mturk_replication.rdata")` and `load("base_categories.rdata")`; the deposited files are `mturk_replication.RData` and `base_categories.RData`. macOS and Windows do not care. Linux does, which is where most people who clone a replication archive today are running it.

With the YouGov file renamed, all three deposited scripts run to completion in a current R and produce their figures. The only warning is `geom_errorbarh()`, deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0. Nothing in the archive writes a file, so running it leaves the deposit untouched, and re-verifying `original/` against the manifest after a full run confirms all `r nrow(manifest)` files unchanged.

### Does the maintained rewrite reproduce the paper?

Yes for everything the paper prints, with exceptions in the observational paragraph on page 5, in one sentence describing Figure 3, and in two sentences describing patterns in the heterogeneous-effects figures.

```{r summary-table}
verdict_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Component,                                        ~Verdict,
  "Table 1 (24 cells plus both totals)",             "Reproduces exactly",
  "Table 1 chi-squared statistic",                   "Reproduces (21.2)",
  "Table 1 chi-squared p-value",                     "Reproduces; the archive's test is an unseeded simulation and 0.002 is inside its range",
  "Text p. 5, 1,010 elections and the 1945 to 2007 span", "Reproduce exactly",
  "Text p. 5, 225 municipalities",                   paste0("Does not reproduce (", dataset$n_municipalities, " here)"),
  "Text p. 5, 779 elections",                        "Reproduces exactly",
  "Text p. 5, 62 and 61 per cent",                   "Reproduce, but the two labels are transposed in the sentence",
  "Text p. 5, p = 0.791",                            paste0("Does not reproduce (", sprintf("%.3f", adv$p_value_hc2), " here)"),
  "Text p. 5, 63 and 48 per cent",                   "Not verifiable; candidate occupation is not in the recovered data",
  "Table A.1 party identification panel and Ns",     "Reproduces exactly",
  "Table A.1 remaining panels",                      "Not verifiable; the deposit carries no other respondent demographics",
  "Figures 3 to 8, B.1, B.2, C.3, C.4",              "Reproduce; all 729 estimates and standard errors agree with the archive to 4e-13",
  "Text on Figure 3, 25 to 30 percentage points",    paste0("Range is tight at both ends; the estimates run ",
                                                            sprintf("%.1f", 100 * min(pol_np$estimate)), " to ",
                                                            sprintf("%.1f", 100 * max(pol_np$estimate))),
  "Text on Figure 3, about 10 percentage points",    "Reproduces (9.1 to 11.7)",
  "Figures 5 and 6, Republicans prefer white candidates", paste0("Holds on YouGov and not on MTurk, where Republicans prefer Asian candidates by ",
                                                                sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mturk_rep_asian$estimate), " points"),
  "Figure 7, Republicans show no competence gap by election type", "Does not hold; the Republican estimate for Mayor excludes zero",
  "Discussion, correlation of 0.95",                 paste0("Reproduces (", sprintf("%.4f", pearson_archive), ") on the archive's specification")
)

k <- kable(verdict_df, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Reproduction verdict by component")
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 8) |>

    column_spec(2, width = "9cm")

```

Every numeric token in the article and the online appendix was extracted by hand into `ground_truth/published_claims.csv`, `r n_extracted` of them, and each classified. `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "pipeline")` are quantities the pipeline should produce, `r sum(published_claims$claim_type == "descriptive")` are claims about shape, sign or ordering that need a computed truth value, and the rest are scale endpoints, category labels, and numbers copied from other papers. The ground truth carries `r n_claims` rows, one for every claim either instrument can reach; `r n_verifiable` of them can be evaluated and `r n_match` come out right. Of the `r n_claims - n_verifiable` that cannot, `r n_archive_locus` are quantities the deposit does not record at all, `r n_no_threshold` are descriptions whose wording sets no threshold to test against, and one is a sentence that names neither a sample nor an election type.

**The article contradicts its own data on `r n_paper_internal` claims.** `r str_to_sentence(spelled(n_paper_internal - n_paper_internal_descriptive))` are misstated numbers and `r spelled(n_paper_internal_descriptive)` are descriptions of the heterogeneous-effects figures that the estimates behind those figures do not support. All `r spelled(n_paper_internal)` are set out in `kirkland_coppock_2018_errata.pdf`, which carries `r n_errata` entries rather than `r spelled(n_paper_internal)`: two of its entries correct a pair of numbers stated in a single sentence.

**The p-value that does not reproduce.** The paper reports that among the 779 elections in which the two candidates had different levels of political experience, the more experienced candidate won about 62 per cent of the time in partisan elections and 61 per cent in nonpartisan elections, and that "this difference is not statistically significant (p = 0.791)." The subset size reproduces exactly, and so do both percentages, though the sentence attaches them to the wrong ballot types: the data give `r sprintf("%.1f", adv$pct_nonpartisan)` per cent nonpartisan and `r sprintf("%.1f", adv$pct_partisan)` per cent partisan. The p-value does not reproduce under any standard test of that comparison. A regression with HC2 errors gives `r sprintf("%.3f", adv$p_value_hc2)`, a chi-squared test gives `r sprintf("%.3f", adv$p_value_chisq)`, and Fisher's exact test, a logit and a t test all land near 0.85. No deposited or recovered script computes this quantity, so there is no code to inspect. The stated conclusion, that the difference is not significant, is unaffected either way: 0.791 and 0.85 lead to the same reading.

**The chi-squared p-value is not a fixed number.** The recovered script calls `chisq.test(simulate.p.value = TRUE)` and sets no seed, so its p-value is a Monte Carlo draw. Over 500 replications of that same call the p-value runs from `r signif(chi$p_simulated_min, 2)` to `r signif(chi$p_simulated_max, 2)`, and `r round(100 * chi$share_rounding_to_0.002)` per cent of draws round to the published 0.002. The published value is a perfectly ordinary draw from the archive's own procedure, not a discrepancy. The asymptotic p-value, which is exact, is `r signif(chi$p_asymptotic, 3)`.

**The correlation of 0.95 depends on an inconsistency inside the archive.** `yougov_replication.R` weights the YouGov main-effects models with the survey weights. `compare_samples_replication.R`, which produces the correlation, refits the same four models without them. The rewrite keeps the archive's unweighted specification, which is what the published `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_archive)` requires: weighting those models instead gives `r sprintf("%.4f", pearson_weighted)`, which rounds to `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_weighted)`.

## Original Archive Reproducibility

**Archive source**: Harvard Dataverse, DOI 10.7910/DVN/WSUHI3, version 1.0, ten files.

```{r repro-table}
repro_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~File,                             ~Status,   ~Issue,
  "mayors_source.R",                 "Runs",    "Helper functions; sourced by every script",
  "mturk_replication.R",             "Runs",    "load() path is mis-cased and would fail on a case-sensitive filesystem; geom_errorbarh() deprecated",
  "yougov_replication.R",            "FAILS",   "load('yougov_replication.rdata'): the deposit contains yougov_replication.xlsx, an RData binary under the wrong extension",
  "compare_samples_replication.R",   "FAILS",   "Same missing file name",
  "observational_replication.R",     "ABSENT",  "Listed in the archive README; not deposited. Recovered from the authors",
  "observational_mayors_replication.rdata", "ABSENT", "Listed in the archive README; not deposited. Recovered from the authors",
  "observational_codebook.txt",      "ABSENT",  "Listed in the archive README; not deposited",
  "CSV copies of the three datasets", "ABSENT", "Listed in the archive README; not deposited"
)

k <- kable(repro_df, booktabs = TRUE,
           caption = "Original archive check (current R environment)")
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 8) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "5cm") |>
    column_spec(2, width = "1.6cm") |>
    column_spec(3, width = "8cm")
}
k
```

**The extension anomaly is visible at the Dataverse level, not just in the download.** The dataset API reports `originalFileName` as `yougov_replication.xlsx` for that file, and Dataverse ingested it into a tabular representation named `yougov_replication.tab`. Whatever the upload looked like, the deposited bytes are an RData file and the name has never matched them. `download_original.R` writes the file under the deposited name and `maintained/helpers.R` loads it under that name, because renaming a deposited file inside a reproduction is how a defect stops being visible to the next reader.

**What the archive computes but the appendix does not print.** Each of the two conjoint scripts contains seven figure blocks. Four correspond to published figures. The remaining three per script build a valence-index analysis, a policy-index analysis and a satisficing analysis, and each script also assembles regression tables it labels D.3, D.5 and so on. The published online appendix has sections A, B and C, no section D, and no valence or policy figures. The paper's Discussion cites "Appendix C.2" for the policy-goal results and "Appendix C.3" for the satisficing results; the appendix as published has neither of those subsections, and its satisficing figures are numbered B.1 and B.2. The online appendix is also dated June 2016, carries a different subtitle from the article, and refers to the main-text conjoint figures as Figures 1 and 2 where the article numbers them 3 and 4. It is an earlier draft of the appendix, published alongside a later draft of the paper.

**Additional patterns** (warnings or fragility, not errors):

- `geom_errorbarh()`, deprecated in ggplot2 4.0.0.
- `position_dodgev()` from `ggstance`, reached through `coefplot`, which the scripts install from GitHub with the comment "it appears that we need version > 1.2.4.9000."
- `gather` / `spread` throughout.
- `rm(list = ls())` at the top of every script.
- The difference-panel coefficients are selected by hardcoded row index (`fit_3_df[19:33, ]`, `[22:39, ]`, `[19:35, ]`, `[22:41, ]`, four different windows), and their labels are then overwritten by assignment from another model's row names. Adding a level to any attribute silently mislabels the entire panel.
- `cl()` recomputes the cluster vector from the unfiltered data, so wherever the outcome has missing values the script has to pass `filter(..., !is.na(comp))` by hand. It does, for the competence figures. Nothing enforces it.

---

## Errata

The rewrite corrects no analytical error in the deposited code, because none of the discrepancies above is one. What the comparison does turn up is `r n_errata` sentences in the article that its own data do not bear out. They are set out in `errata.qmd`, which renders to `kirkland_coppock_2018_errata.pdf` at the repository root, ordered by severity. Every corrected value in that note is computed at render time from `maintained/output/`, so it cannot go stale in the way the article did. None of the `r spelled(n_errata)` changes a conclusion.

**`r str_to_sentence(spelled(n_errata_numeric))` are misstated numbers.** The two ballot types are transposed in the experience-advantage comparison, so the sentence reports the gap running against the paper's own argument. The p-value of 0.791 on that comparison reproduces under no test. The mayoral dataset covers `r dataset$n_municipalities` municipalities rather than 225. And the range of political experience effects in the sentence describing Figure 3 is wrong at both ends.

**`r str_to_sentence(spelled(n_errata_descriptive))` are descriptions the estimates do not support.** A description a reader would quote misleads exactly as a number does, so these are entries in the note rather than observations about it; the corrected sentence says what the estimates support and the reason line carries the evidence.

- "Republican respondents marginally prefer white candidates while Democrats marginally prefer nonwhite candidates" holds in the YouGov sample, where all three Republican nonwhite estimates are negative. It reverses on MTurk, where Republican respondents prefer Asian candidates to white candidates by `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mturk_rep_asian$estimate)` percentage points while preferring white candidates to Black and Hispanic ones.
- "Democratic respondents (but not Republican respondents) rate such candidates as even more competent in the absence of party labels" reads the difference column of Figure 7 as null for Republicans. `r str_to_sentence(spelled(n_clears_dem))` of the `r spelled(n_per_party)` Democratic intervals exclude zero, and so does `r spelled(n_clears_rep)` of the `r spelled(n_per_party)` Republican ones, for candidates who have been mayor.

**One claim the article's data cannot judge either way is deliberately not in the note.** "Democrats are 10 percentage points more likely to choose a female candidate than a male candidate" names neither a sample nor an election type, and the four estimates it could be reporting run 3.4 to 11.1 percentage points. That is unjudgeable rather than wrong, and the ground truth records it as `unresolved`.

---

## Ground Truth Verification

The ground truth carries one row per claim either instrument can reach: `r n_claims` rows against the `r n_extracted` numeric tokens extracted from the article and appendix. The claims left out are scale endpoints and category labels the deposit cannot reach, and numbers the article takes from other papers; they are recorded in `published_claims.csv` and verified against the sources they come from.

```{r gt-summary-table}
gt_summary <- gt |>
  mutate(Verdict = case_when(match_rewrite == 1 ~ "Matches",
                             match_rewrite == 0 ~ "Does not match",
                             .default = "Not evaluable")) |>
  count(`Table or figure` = table_figure, Verdict) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = Verdict, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

k <- kable(gt_summary, booktabs = TRUE,
           caption = paste0("Ground truth verification by component (", nrow(gt), " rows)"))
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 8) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "7cm")
}
k
```

Every row that does not match, or that could not be evaluated for a reason specific to it, is below. The `r n_a1_absent` Table A.1 cells the deposit cannot reach share one reason between them and are counted in the table above rather than listed one line each.

```{r gt-detail-table}
k <- gt |>
  filter(match_rewrite == 0 |
           (is.na(match_rewrite) & !str_starts(claim_id, "table_a1_"))) |>
  transmute(Claim = claim, Published = replace_na(value_paper, "--"),
            Pipeline = if_else(is.na(value_rewrite), "--",
                               formatC(value_rewrite, format = "fg", digits = 4)),
            Locus = replace_na(defect_locus, "--")) |>
  kable(booktabs = TRUE,
        caption = "Every claim that does not reproduce, and every one that cannot be evaluated")
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 7) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "8cm")
}
k
```

**Summary**: `r n_match` of `r n_verifiable` evaluable claims match the published values; `r n_miss` do not. `ground_truth/build_ground_truth.R` rebuilds this table from `maintained/output/` at the end of every run. The only numbers typed into that script are the published values themselves, which serve as comparison targets and are never inputs to a computation.

**The archive columns are empty, and this repository is missing the script that would fill them.** `value_script` and `match` are `NA` on every row. The deposited scripts write no files at all, keeping every result as an in-memory R object, as the archive's own README explains, so recovering an archive number means running the deposited code in a scratch copy and harvesting the objects it leaves behind. That is the job of a `ground_truth/extract_archive_values.R`, and **this repository does not have one yet**. Until it does, the comparison recorded here is between the article and the maintained rewrite, which is what `value_rewrite` and `match_rewrite` carry. The one place the archive's own output has been compared directly is the 729 figure estimates described under Figure Verification, and that comparison lives in no committed script either.

Filling `value_script` from `value_rewrite` would make the column look populated while recording the rewrite's own numbers as the archive's, which is worse than leaving it empty. It is left empty, and the gap is stated here rather than implied.

## Maintained Rewrite

The rewrite lives in `maintained/`: a shared `helpers.R`, one script per published table or figure, four for in-text quantities, and the claims file that prints every published number beside the sentence that states it.

```{r scripts-table}
scripts_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Script,                                        ~Output,
  "helpers.R",                                    "Packages, both datasets, the estimation and plotting helpers",
  "table_1_observational_experience.R",           "output/table_1_observational_experience.csv, output/text_observational_chisq.csv, output/text_observational_dataset_description.csv",
  "table_a1_party_identification.R",              "output/table_a1_party_identification.csv",
  "figure_3_mturk_main_candidate_pref.R",         "output/figure_3_mturk_main_candidate_pref.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_4_yougov_main_candidate_pref.R",        "output/figure_4_yougov_main_candidate_pref.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_5_mturk_het_fx_candidate_pref.R",       "output/figure_5_mturk_het_fx_candidate_pref.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_6_yougov_het_fx_candidate_pref.R",      "output/figure_6_yougov_het_fx_candidate_pref.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_7_mturk_het_fx_competence.R",           "output/figure_7_mturk_het_fx_competence.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_8_yougov_het_fx_competence.R",          "output/figure_8_yougov_het_fx_competence.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_b1_mturk_satisficing.R",                "output/figure_b1_mturk_satisficing.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_b2_yougov_satisficing.R",               "output/figure_b2_yougov_satisficing.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_c3_mturk_main_competence.R",            "output/figure_c3_mturk_main_competence.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "figure_c4_yougov_main_competence.R",           "output/figure_c4_yougov_main_competence.{pdf,png,csv}",
  "text_design_parameters.R",                     "output/text_design_parameters.csv",
  "text_observational_experience_advantage.R",    "output/text_observational_experience_advantage.csv",
  "text_mturk_yougov_correlation.R",              "output/text_mturk_yougov_correlation.{csv,pdf,png}",

k <- kable(scripts_df, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Maintained rewrite scripts")
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 8) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "6cm") |>
    column_spec(2, width = "9cm")
}

```

**Key substitutions**:

```{r subst-table}
subst_df <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Original,                                       ~Rewrite,
  "rm(list = ls())",                               "removed",
  "library() in each script",                      "source(helpers.R); all packages in helpers.R",
  "custom cl() over sandwich and lmtest",          "lm_robust(clusters = , se_type = 'stata'), identical to 1e-15",
  "coefficient rows selected by index",            "filter(str_detect(term, ':nonpartisan$'))",
  "labels reassigned from another model's rownames", "labels derived from each model's own terms",
  "position_dodgev() from ggstance via coefplot",  "position_dodge(width = 0.5)",
  "geom_errorbarh(height = 0)",                    "geom_linerange()",
  "geom_segment() for confidence bars",            "geom_linerange()",
  "gather / spread",                               "pivot_longer / pivot_wider",
  "magrittr pipe",                                 "native pipe",
  "figures held only as in-memory R objects",      "written to output/ as PDF, PNG and CSV",
  "load('yougov_replication.rdata')",              "load('yougov_replication.xlsx'), the deposited name"
)

k <- kable(subst_df, booktabs = TRUE, caption = "Deprecated patterns and replacements")
if (latex_out) {
  k <- k |>
    kable_styling(latex_options = c("striped", "hold_position"), font_size = 8) |>
    column_spec(1, width = "7cm") |>
    column_spec(2, width = "8cm")
}
k
```

**The standard error substitution.** The archive's `cl()` function scales the CR0 meat by `(M / (M - 1)) * ((N - 1) / (N - K))`, which is what `estimatr::lm_robust(se_type = "stata")` computes. The two agree to 1e-15 on every model in the paper. An earlier version of this rewrite asked for `se_type = "CR1S"`, the name estimatr used for the same estimator until version 1.0.6 retired it; that name now raises an error, which is why every figure script here names the estimator "stata".

**The weighting decisions are surfaced, not defaulted.** The archive applies the YouGov survey weights to the main-effects figures (4 and C.4) and to the satisficing figure (B.2), but not to the heterogeneous-effects figures (6 and 8) and not to the four models behind the correlation in the Discussion. The rewrite reproduces each figure as the archive specifies it, and `election_type_panels()` takes `weighted` as a required argument with no default so the choice is visible at every call site. Weighting the heterogeneous-effects models would move individual estimates by up to 0.04 and the reported correlation from `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_archive)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", pearson_weighted)`, which is a change to the analysis rather than a repair to it.

**What the rewrite adds.** The published appendix figures B.1 and B.2, which the archive computes and no earlier rewrite covered, and the one panel of Table A.1 the deposit can support. The in-text observational comparison on page 5 has no code anywhere in the archive or the recovered files; it is reconstructed here from the recovered data. `text_design_parameters.R` reads back the design facts the article states in prose (elections per subject, attributes per election type, the age levels, the endpoints of the competence scale) rather than leaving them asserted. Every figure now writes a CSV of the plotted estimates alongside the image, which is what makes a rerun diffable.

**The policy-goal analysis is rewritten even though it was never published.** The Mechanism section reports results for a policy-goal index and cites "Appendix C.2" for them. There is no Appendix C.2: the published appendix has sections A, B and C only, C has no subsections, and the policy-goal analysis appears nowhere in it. Both deposited scripts compute it, so `text_policy_index_het_fx.R` reproduces those models and the two sentences the article bases on them can be checked. The index's direction is documented nowhere, and the appendix section that would have defined it does not exist, so the candidate's own party label is used as the anchor: a Republican candidate raises the index and a Democratic candidate lowers it in every sample by respondent party cell, which fixes the high end as the conservative end. Read that way both sentences hold.

**What the rewrite leaves alone.** The confidence bars are drawn at plus or minus 1.96 standard errors, as the archive draws them, rather than at a t quantile on the cluster-adjusted degrees of freedom. The valence-index analysis the archive computes is not rewritten, since no sentence in the article or the appendix refers to it. The unweighted YouGov specifications stay unweighted.

## Figure Verification

Every plotted coefficient and standard error in the ten conjoint figures was compared against the archive's own `lm()` plus `cl()` output, term by term and panel by panel: 729 pairs, agreeing to within 4e-13. Two of the figures follow.

```{r fig3-embed, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Figure 3 reproduction. MTurk main analysis, candidate preference. Columns are nonpartisan elections, partisan elections, and the difference between them; rows are attribute groups. Political experience carries visibly more weight when the party label is withheld."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig_img("figure_3_mturk_main_candidate_pref"))
```

```{r fig5-embed, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Figure 5 reproduction. MTurk heterogeneous effects on candidate preference, Democratic respondents in blue and Republican respondents in red."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig_img("figure_5_mturk_het_fx_candidate_pref"))
```

```{r figb1-embed, out.width="95%", fig.cap="Appendix Figure B.1 reproduction, the satisficing check. Partisan elections only, split by whether the two candidates share a party. Both panels display six attributes, so the number of attributes is held fixed and only the informativeness of the party label varies."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig_img("figure_b1_mturk_satisficing"))
```

```{r corr-embed, out.width="70%", fig.cap="The Discussion's correlation of 0.95, plotted. Each point is one attribute level's effect on candidate preference, estimated on MTurk and on YouGov, with 95 per cent intervals on both axes."}
knitr::include_graphics(fig_img("text_mturk_yougov_correlation"))
```

## In-Text Claims

`maintained/in_text_claims.R` carries one block per published claim: the article's sentence verbatim in a comment, then code that reads `maintained/output/` and prints the number in the article's own units and rounding. It never fits a model and never reads the ground truth. It reaches the same quantities as `build_ground_truth.R` by its own route through the same output files, so a disagreement between the two is a finding rather than a coincidence.

Descriptive claims get a computed truth value rather than a number, and the evidence behind it is printed on the line beneath. A claim that reduces to a boolean gets a verdict; "relatively muted", "similarly small" and "do not differ much" set no threshold, so those blocks print the distribution and no verdict, because a verdict would invent the threshold the sentence withholds.

Coverage is a gate rather than a convention. Each claim prints one line of the form `CLAIM <id> = <value> || <label>`, and that printed line is the only link between a block and the extraction. `build_ground_truth.R` runs the claims file non-interactively, reads the ids back off the lines it actually printed, and halts unless every pipeline and descriptive row of `published_claims.csv` appears among them, unless every id printed is one the article makes, and unless each has a ground truth row. Nothing in the gate parses a comment: a comment naming the claims a block covers would prove only that someone wrote the comment, and it can go stale on its own while the code beside it changes.

---

## Maintained Rewrite Verification

Two full runs of `run_all.R` produce byte-identical CSV and PNG output. Only the PDF figures differ between runs, because a PDF records the time it was written.
